clue.text: A third identity concealed by syndicate

definitions.note: Yorkshire was historically divided into three administrative parts, each one a third of the county

indicators.note: concealed by says one piece is hidden inside the other

parts.note: a ring is a group working together, like a syndicate
ID is the usual short form of identity

explanation.surface: Someone's identity is kept secret by a business syndicate, a third of whose members know it.
explanation.walkthrough: The RIDINGS were the three divisions of old Yorkshire, an English county; the name comes from an Old Norse word for 'third part'.
explanation.definitionFit: Historical division: each Yorkshire riding was one of three parts of the county.

clue.text: A spider in trouble — 'e disappears in fast flowing water

indicators.note: letters that are in trouble are thrown into disorder and rearranged, with one letter disappearing

parts.note: the dropped h of Cockney speech turns he into 'e, and the clue uses it for the letter E

explanation.surface: A spider struggling in a torrent, with a Cockney exclamation about it vanishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in trouble' scrambles A SPIDER; 'disappears' then removes the E, which the clue names with the Cockney ''e'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapids are stretches of a river where the current runs swift over rocks.

clue.text: Religious person in the WI

definitions.meaning: a friar of the order founded by St Dominic
describing someone or something from Dominica or the ... Republic, in the West Indies

explanation.surface: A churchgoer who belongs to the Women's Institute.
explanation.walkthrough: The WI looks like Britain's Women's Institute, a village-based women's club; here it is the West Indies.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a member of St Dominic's friar order, and an adjective for the Caribbean island nations.

clue.text: With absence of churchgoers initially change part of service

parts.note: with absence of something means there is none of it

indicators.note: initially means only the opening letter of the word is used

parts.note: to turn is to change, as milk turns

explanation.surface: With no churchgoers at the start, part of the service has to be altered.
explanation.definitionFit: Liturgical term: a section of the night office of matins in monastic worship.

clue.text: Familiar OT book returning saint carried around Surrey town

indicators.note: carried around says the reversed letters go round the town, one at each end
returning means the abbreviation for saint is read backwards

parts.note: Woking is a commuter town in Surrey, south-west of London

explanation.surface: A saint carries a well-known Old Testament book around a Surrey town.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is a county south-west of London. 'returning' turns the saint's letters round before 'carried around' wraps them about the town, one at each end.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical book is commonly cited by its numbered name, so it is a well-known Old Testament title.

clue.text: Fatwa, terrible, may be seen as such a sign

definitions.text: Fatwa, terrible, may be seen as such a sign

parts.words: Fatwa, terrible, may be seen as such a sign
parts.note: the phrase fatwa terrible carries a liquid inside it, the letters running across its two words, so it can be called a carrier of that liquid, a zodiac sign

explanation.surface: A dreadful religious ruling might be read as an omen.
explanation.walkthrough: Look across the join of 'fatWA TERrible': the words hold WATER, so the phrase is a holder of water, Aquarius in the zodiac.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquarius, the eleventh zodiac sign, is pictured as a figure pouring from a jug.

clue.text: One of the ancestral spirits, thousand over a huge country

indicators.note: in a down clue, over puts the first piece above the rest

parts.note: K stands for a thousand, as in 10K
China is one of the largest countries on earth

explanation.surface: A thousand ancestral spirits hover over a vast nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopi and Pueblo religion: kachinas are spirit beings, often of ancestors, represented by dolls and masked dancers.

clue.text: Name given to Scottish child not born in a Scottish town

indicators.note: given to says the abbreviation is attached to the front of what follows
not says the letter for born is removed

parts.note: bairn is the Scots word for a child
B is the abbreviation for born, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A name is given to a Scottish child who was born elsewhere, not in a certain town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes B (born) from BAIRN, Scots for child. NAIRN is a seaside town near Inverness.
explanation.definitionFit: Geography: a small coastal burgh on the Moray Firth in the Highlands.

clue.text: Audibly making reference to an observation

indicators.note: audibly says the word for the clue phrase is to be heard, not written

parts.note: citing a source is making reference to it

explanation.surface: Someone loudly mentions a thing they have observed.
explanation.definitionFit: A sighting is an instance of seeing something, like a reported UFO spotting.

clue.text: Pulpy stuff available from flower club

parts.note: a flower is something that flows, a river, and the Po is Italy's longest river
a mace is a heavy club used as a weapon

explanation.surface: Mushy material on offer from a florists' society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' and 'club' look like a gardening society, but the flower is a river (something that flows).
explanation.definitionFit: Cider-making term: the crushed apple pulp left after pressing.

clue.text: Stage show about one of the 4 in building

indicators.note: about means the show's title is turned round

parts.note: Cats is the long-running Lloyd Webber musical
the solution at 4 across names two monarchs, so one of them is a king

explanation.surface: A theatre production about one of four people in a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses CATS, the musical, giving STAC; '4' points to 4 across, whose two monarchs give KING.
explanation.definitionFit: Piling things up on one another is a way of building, as with stacking bricks.

clue.text: One condemns squalid quarters used by wild cat, right?

parts.note: a den is a squalid or wretched place to live
the ounce is the snow leopard

explanation.surface: Someone criticises filthy lodgings taken over by a feral cat, asking if that is correct.
explanation.walkthrough: The OUNCE is another name for the snow leopard, a wild cat of Central Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: Agent noun: a person who publicly condemns or informs against others.

clue.text: Work leaders may have gone out with hard cash but no love

indicators.note: out describes the letters as gone astray, so they are to be rearranged

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, which is the letter O

explanation.surface: Foremen might have walked off with the hard cash, leaving no affection behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' scrambles GONE plus HARD CASH; 'but no love' says an O is left over, so the remaining letters make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Industrial term: a chargehand is a worker in charge of a small team, below a foreman.

clue.text: Is it not common, the thing behind the bar?

definitions.note: a common, informal shortening of 'isn't it', used as a tag question

indicators.note: behind puts the second piece after the pub

parts.note: an inn is a pub, where there is a bar
it is a word for a thing

explanation.surface: Asking whether the item behind the pub counter is ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'common' here means vulgar or slangy speech, describing the tag, not ordinariness.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang contraction: a tag question used in casual British speech in place of 'isn't it'.

clue.text: Two Conservatives worried by country — it's one thing after the other

parts.note: CON and C are both abbreviations for Conservative
ate in the sense of gnawed at or troubled, as in what's eating you
a nation is a country

explanation.surface: A pair of Tory politicians fretting about the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' gives ATE, the past of eat in its 'trouble' sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A chain of linked events, each following the last in sequence.

clue.text: Impropriety around Christmas time? Nothing odd!

parts.note: in December, written in short
nothing is zero, the letter O
rum means odd or peculiar

explanation.surface: Bad behaviour at Christmas time? Nothing strange in that.
explanation.walkthrough: RUM as 'odd' is British informal usage, as in 'a rum business'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: lack of decorum, behaviour that breaks good manners.

clue.text: Maybe put a tick against what playwright sounds like?

indicators.note: sounds like says the dramatist's name is heard, not spelt

parts.note: Anton Chekhov, Russian dramatist of The Cherry Orchard

explanation.surface: Perhaps marking off whatever the dramatist resembles.
explanation.definitionFit: Phrasal verb: to mark an item on a list as done, often with a tick.

clue.text: Possibility of thin gnu where pursuers operate

parts.note: read the first word of the answer as an anagram of thin gnu, and the second as the signal: ground up, those letters could form it

explanation.surface: A skinny wildebeest might be found where the hunters are.
explanation.walkthrough: Read in reverse: 'ground' (crushed) is an anagram signal, and HUNTING ground (mixed) can produce THIN GNU, so the answer is one possibility for that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a place where hunters, or anyone seeking something, look for their quarry.

clue.text: Making some complaint, one definitely sounded like the vicar?

indicators.note: Making some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A churchgoer grumbles that someone definitely sounded like a clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: Vicars traditionally chant prayers in a level recitative tone, so to speak like one is to chant.

clue.text: Story book under domestic fixture I pulled out

indicators.note: in a down clue, under puts the book below the first piece
pulled out says the letter I is removed

parts.note: a unit is a fitted cupboard, as in a kitchen unit
Ruth is a book of the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A book is put beneath a fitted cupboard, from which I've pulled something out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Story' is used in its sense of a fib.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal sense: a story can be a lie, as in 'don't tell stories'.

clue.text: Coarse times full of beastly sounds

indicators.note: full of says the first piece is filled by the other

parts.note: by means times in multiplication, as in four by two
lows are the sounds cattle make

explanation.surface: Rough days filled with animal noises.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: blowsy means coarse and slovenly, especially in looks.

clue.text: Guile about a lot of things?

parts.note: C, for circa, means about
a raft of things is a large number of them

explanation.surface: Cunning concerning a great many matters.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: craft as cunning or artful deceit.

clue.text: Wood that's mottled first to be discarded

indicators.note: first to be discarded says the opening letter is removed

parts.note: dapple means spotted or mottled

explanation.surface: Speckled timber whose first piece is thrown away.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the timber of the fruit tree, used in furniture and for smoking food.

clue.text: Ambassador trounced article opposing the official line

parts.note: HE, His Excellency, is the title of an ambassador

indicators.note: trounced means beaten up, so the letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A diplomat demolished a newspaper piece that went against government policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trounced' scrambles ARTICLE into RETICAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: dissenting from accepted doctrine, as a heretic does.

clue.text: Writer needing time, keeping on after work from rival

indicators.note: after puts the writer piece behind the work

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a work

indicators.note: keeping says the writer and time hold the next word inside

parts.note: a pen is a writing implement
taken as written

explanation.surface: An author needs time to keep going after finishing work by a competitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' puts ON inside PENT to give PONENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an adversary or competitor in a contest.

clue.text: Quarrel about unethical use of animal material? It's groovy!

definitions.note: something with a groove in it, a channel

parts.note: fur is the coat of an animal used for clothing
a row is a quarrel; the phrase describes a dispute over animal pelts

explanation.surface: An argument about wearing animal skins turns out to be cool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'groovy' looks like 60s slang for great; it is literal, full of grooves.
explanation.definitionFit: A furrow is a trench or channel, such as one cut by a plough.

clue.text: Very hard one to complete, outwardly brill?

indicators.note: outwardly says the fish is on the outside of the other pieces

parts.note: brill is a flatfish
I is the Roman numeral for one
to end is to complete

explanation.surface: A puzzle that's very hard to finish, yet looks brilliant on the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brill' looks like slang for brilliant; it is a flatfish.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal sense: fiendish means extremely difficult, like a devilish puzzle.

clue.text: Bad spell that's reduced London football team? Gosh!

indicators.note: reduced says the club's name is cut down, losing a middle stretch

parts.note: West Ham United is an east London football club
my is an exclamation of surprise, like gosh

explanation.surface: A cut-down London football club suffers a bad run, oh dear!
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' cuts EST from WEST HAM, an east London football club, leaving WHAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal: a whammy is an evil spell or jinx, as in a double whammy.
